abstract.t: PulseBeam nodes use Chitchat to maintain local observations of the nodes in one cluster. This document specifies configuration, durable node identity, incarnation selection, snapshot consumption, and eligibility for new work. It also specifies the server lifecycle changes needed to withdraw admission safely while peers may still observe an earlier readiness advertisement.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: Membership gives a cluster control-plane component a way to enumerate candidate nodes using its own observation of gossip. A candidate is identified by a process incarnation so that a restart can invalidate stale observations of the previous process. The destination independently decides whether to admit work.

This is an internal PulseBeam specification. Configuration, identity allocation, gossip, metadata replacement, snapshots, and membership supervision describe the current implementation. defines the proposed lifecycle publisher and admission contract. Today the clustered server starts membership with empty application metadata and provides observations only.

Each configured cluster is an independent gossip domain. The cluster-wide inputs and outputs in this document are scoped to that domain. WAN discovery, inter-node RPC and data transport, placement and ownership, resource discovery, and session migration have separate contracts under .
The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "SHOULD", and "MAY" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.

section.name: Configuration and Bootstrap
section.t: The Linux server opts in through a [cluster] configuration section or NodeBuilder::with_cluster. A standalone server opens no gossip socket, creates no membership task, and does not touch membership identity state. The server owns configuration, name resolution, the UDP socket, the identity lease, and supervision. The control-side membership service owns the Chitchat task and snapshot publication.

dl.dd: An exact string shared by peers in a gossip domain. It is 1 to 128 UTF-8 bytes, contains no control characters, and cannot consist entirely of whitespace. Operators MUST assign different IDs to distinct gossip domains sharing network reachability.
A unicast or wildcard bind address with a nonzero UDP port. The server default is 0.0.0.0:7946.

An explicit, peer-reachable IP and the listen port. The server accepts an IP or a hostname for advertise_host. A hostname must resolve at startup to exactly one distinct address. Wildcard, multicast, IPv4 broadcast, and IPv6 link-local endpoints are invalid as advertisements or seeds. Listen, advertise, and seed addresses use the same IP family. The advertised UDP address is for gossip.

Zero or more ordinary peers in this cluster, each configured as a socket address or a host and port that resolves unambiguously at startup. An empty list permits a first node or a node discoverable through inbound gossip. A joining node and the intended cluster discover each other when either side initiates gossip over a working network path. With no reachable seed and no inbound contact, the node remains isolated. Bootstrap requires neither a quorum nor a response from a particular seed. Loss of a seed does not invalidate other known peers.
An explicitly configured, private, writable, durable directory dedicated to this logical node. The server requires --data-dir with [cluster].

section.t: The server rejects invalid configuration, ambiguous resolution, identity allocation errors, or socket bind errors at startup. It validates the supplied socket against the configured listen address. It can start with no reachable peer. A successful start establishes local membership service availability.

For example, configure this node in cluster.toml and start the server with pulsebeam --config ./cluster.toml --data-dir ./state/node-a alongside the normal server authentication and media configuration.
Use the node's own reachable address and private state directory in each deployment.

section.name: Identity and Incarnations
section.t: A NodeId identifies a logical server across process restarts. Its canonical text is n_0 followed by the 26 uppercase Crockford Base32 characters emitted by the shared PulseBeam ID codec for a UUIDv7. A generation is a positive unsigned 64-bit integer allocated by that node's host. The local observation key, called an incarnation, is (NodeId, generation, advertised gossip socket address).

For a fresh state directory, the first allocation creates a new ID and generation 1. For existing state, the server keeps the ID and increments the stored generation. The host MUST commit the allocation durably before sending gossip. Each new process allocation uses a higher generation for a retained ID. Failed startups may consume a generation. Changing the advertised socket address for a retained ID requires a new generation.

The Linux server takes the exclusive lock on membership.lock, validates the version-1 JSON record in membership-state.json, and stages the increment in membership-state.next. It syncs the replacement, atomically renames it over the state record, and syncs the directory before returning the allocation. The lock covers socket lifetime, including canceled startup. A locked directory, malformed or unsupported record, generation zero, overflow, or a read, write, or sync failure prevents joining. The state record contains version (the integer 1), node_id (the node ID string), and generation (the committed integer). Unknown fields and records larger than 4,096 bytes are rejected. An interrupted staged replacement is discarded during the next allocation under the lock.

Operators MUST preserve current state for a retained identity and MUST NOT clone or roll back identity state. If durable state is lost, provision a fresh directory and let the server allocate a new logical ID. The directory lock provides exclusion for processes using that directory. Incarnation history provides bounded observations of supersession at each observer. Neither supplies distributed fencing.

section.name: Gossip and Metadata
section.t: The implementation uses unmodified Chitchat 0.13.0, wire protocol V0, over UDP. The Chitchat ID carries the canonical node ID, generation, and advertised address. The gossip interval is one second. Membership reconciles the complete local protocol view on its own one-second interval and after a local metadata write. Chitchat's default failure detector applies, including its 24-hour dead-node grace. Deleted metadata keys use a 15-minute tombstone grace. These timers govern local protocol behavior and retention. End-to-end observation of a change depends on gossip delivery and scheduling.

The protocol-owned key pb.schema has the exact string value 1. An application key K is carried as meta.K and exposed as K in the local API. The application map has at most 16 entries. Keys contain 1 to 64 ASCII bytes in A-Z, a-z, 0-9, ., _, or -. Values are UTF-8 strings of at most 1,024 bytes. The sum of unprefixed key and value lengths is at most 8,192 bytes. Keys outside the application prefix are excluded from the application map.

Handle::replace_metadata validates and submits the complete local map. An invalid request leaves the map unchanged. The service serializes accepted writes, removes previously present keys omitted from a replacement, and reconciles its own snapshot before acknowledging success. Acknowledgement covers local application and observation. Remote observers may see changes later or skip intermediate values. A caller that stops waiting after enqueueing cannot infer that its write was canceled.

A node MUST serialize full-map replacements through one owner of the desired map when several local components contribute metadata. Replacing one field MUST preserve all other desired fields. Lifecycle owns lifecycle, the sole application key standardized here.

section.name: Liveness and Supported Records
section.t: Each observer builds its own snapshot from one coherent read of Chitchat state. Records with an unparseable node ID or generation zero are omitted. Each remaining record exposes the following liveness, independent of schema support and incarnation status.

dl.dd: Present in protocol state and in neither the live nor suspected sets.
Present in the observer's Chitchat live set.
Outside the live set and classified by Chitchat as dead or scheduled for deletion.

section.t: A record is supported if its advertised address satisfies the endpoint rules, pb.schema is exactly 1, and its application metadata satisfies . Unsupported records remain visible with an empty application map. A record is usable exactly when it is supported, Live, current by generation, and free of an address conflict.

section.name: Supersession, Conflicts, and Retention

ol.li: For each node ID, track the highest observed valid generation. Observations with unsupported metadata or unusable addresses still contribute evidence. A lower generation is superseded even if live and even if every record of the higher generation is suspected or unsupported.

Different advertised addresses observed for the same ID and generation are an address conflict. Mark both while both records are present. For the highest generation, retain the conflict even if one or both addresses disappear. A higher generation starts its own conflict history.

Refresh the high-water record while its highest generation is present in protocol state. Retain it for 48 hours from the last such observation. Older generations do not refresh that timer. After expiration on reconciliation, current protocol records can establish a new high-water record. A fresh observer also starts with empty history.

section.t: For example, if generation 8 is suspected and generation 7 still appears live, neither is usable. If generation 9 then appears on two addresses, neither address is usable even after one disappears from protocol state. A supported, live generation 10 at one address can become usable. This behavior rules out fallback based on information still held by this observer.

Loss and partitions can produce different views, false suspicions, or loss of every remote candidate. When communication resumes, current state can propagate and previously suspected nodes can become live. There is no bound on wall-clock convergence and no agreement barrier. An observer that restarted or forgot its high-water record may recognize replayed old evidence as current. Consumers MUST NOT use liveness, removal, or supersession alone to authorize work, take ownership, or conclude that another process has stopped.

section.name: Snapshots and Subscription
section.t: Handle::snapshot returns a complete owned local snapshot. It contains a local revision, a map of incarnation records, a map of retained highest generations by node ID, and a list of changes relative to the preceding revision. An ID can remain in the high-water map after all of its incarnation records have been removed. A record's removal indicates its absence from local protocol state.

The first published snapshot has revision 1. Within an observer process the revision increases when either map changes, with no new revision for a no-op reconciliation. Revisions reset with the observer and cannot be compared across observers. Joined and Removed refer to incarnation-map entries. Liveness, Metadata, and Status describe changes within an existing entry. Incarnation describes an addition, change, or removal in the highest-generation map.

Handle::subscribe returns a watch receiver. A consumer MUST reconcile from the initial complete snapshot and the latest complete snapshot on each wakeup. Notifications may coalesce. The change list can be used as an optimization only when the previous processed revision is the immediate predecessor from the same observer. When a subscription closes, a consumer MUST invalidate its candidate cache until it obtains a snapshot from a running service.

section.name: Lifecycle State Machine
section.t: The server lifecycle owns the local admission gate. The membership service distributes the gate's lifecycle state as meta.lifecycle on the wire. The exact, case-sensitive values and transitions are defined below. For this contract, new work is the creation of a new assignment directed to a node selected using cluster membership. The operation's existing authorization, capacity, and transport checks still apply.

dl.dd: Initial state of every incarnation. Local admission is closed. Include this value in initial gossip metadata. The node may advance to ready or go directly to draining on shutdown.

Membership is running, the handlers that commit new assignments are serving, and the resources they require are initialized. The lifecycle owner MUST keep admission closed until these conditions hold, then open the gate before publishing ready. The first gossip tick, socket bind, or receipt of a peer announcement cannot by itself establish readiness. No particular peer count or remote snapshot is required.

Terminal lifecycle value for this incarnation. Local admission is closed. Existing accepted work follows the host shutdown path. A node that must withdraw readiness after entering service enters draining. Returning to service uses a new process incarnation beginning in starting.

section.t: The server MUST serialize lifecycle transitions and order their metadata replacements so an earlier ready write cannot replace a later draining write. Repeated readiness and shutdown triggers are idempotent. If shutdown races readiness, the lifecycle owner MUST close the gate and prevent it from reopening for that incarnation. A ready update already submitted to membership may still become visible before draining.

section.name: Candidate Selection and Local Admission
section.t: A consumer selecting a destination for new work MUST require both Member::is_usable() and the exact application metadata value lifecycle=ready in the same snapshot. A missing key, unknown value, or any other lifecycle state yields an ineligible record. The consumer retains the selected incarnation for the attempt. It MUST NOT fall back to an older generation to find a ready record.

Before committing a new assignment, the destination MUST verify that the request or its bound transport context targets its own cluster ID, node ID, and generation and that its local admission gate is open. The gossip address identifies observations and conveys no authority for assignment. The inter-node transport contract supplies the encoding or binding for this identity check. The gate check and assignment commit MUST be ordered against gate closure so any assignment admitted before closure counts as existing work, and any attempt that commits after closure is rejected. Remote readiness never opens the local gate.

On rejection, target mismatch, or a failed connection, a consumer MAY reconsider the latest snapshot under its own retry policy and the operation's own idempotency rules. Membership supplies neither a reservation nor an outcome for a timed-out attempt. A change in candidate eligibility by itself does not revoke an existing assignment.

section.name: Graceful Shutdown and Failure

ol.li: On shutdown or withdrawal of readiness, close local admission and enter draining. A request using a stale remote ready view must now fail local admission.

Submit a complete metadata replacement advertising draining while gossip is still running. The host MUST enforce a finite drain budget measured on its monotonic clock from gate closure. The host supplies the budget according to the work it admits. Metadata acknowledgement and remote observation MUST NOT delay local drain or extend this budget.

Keep gossip active while the host drains previously admitted work. If the budget expires first, the host MUST terminate the remaining work. Once work finishes or is terminated, cancel and join membership. Keep the identity lease until the gossip socket closes. There is no reliable leave handshake. An observer that misses the drain update learns of loss through Chitchat suspicion and cleanup.

section.t: If publishing ready fails, the server MUST close admission and begin shutdown. If publishing draining fails or cannot finish within the host's shutdown budget, the server MUST keep admission closed and continue shutdown. A fatal socket or membership task failure, including unexpected task termination, MUST cause the server to stop admission and shut down. A crash may skip all graceful steps. Releasing gossip after a graceful drain is a local resource cleanup step and makes no claim about remote state.

section.name: Compatibility and Rollout
section.t: The lifecycle key is additive under pb.schema=1. Older observers continue to evaluate generic membership usability. A lifecycle-aware consumer treats a legacy publisher with no lifecycle key as ineligible for new work. An unknown schema makes the whole record unsupported while retaining valid identity evidence. An unknown lifecycle value leaves generic usability intact and makes the record ineligible for new work.

Upgrade clustered servers to publish lifecycle and enforce local admission before enabling membership-based work assignment. Confirm sufficient eligible capacity from each selecting node's own snapshot before activating assignment. During a mixed deployment, only upgraded publishers that advertise ready and pass the ordinary usability checks become eligible. A rollback that removes the lifecycle-aware admission path MUST first withdraw the instance through that path and stop it before starting the legacy binary. Once a selector observes the replacement generation, the old generation is superseded and the legacy publisher remains ineligible. Standalone admission is outside this membership contract.

section.name: Operation and Verification
section.t: Use a reachable private address and dedicated identity state per node. The startup log identifies the allocated node ID, generation, and advertised gossip socket. For failed bootstrap, check cluster ID, IP family, seed reachability, and the UDP path before interpreting absence as failure. For persistent ineligibility, inspect the complete local snapshot for the highest generation, liveness, schema support, conflicts, and lifecycle. For a same-generation conflict, establish which deployment owns the durable identity before restarting it with a higher generation. Reprovision a cloned deployment with a new ID.

The existing executable checks cover configuration, identity persistence and locking, metadata validation, observation semantics, and deterministic gossip scenarios. Run the membership owner checks and existing simulator with . Lifecycle implementation is complete when deterministic tests through the server lifecycle and gossip exercise these additional cases.

ul.li: starting stays ineligible despite live gossip. ready is published after local admission opens. Missing and unknown lifecycle values stay ineligible.

Hold back drain gossip and attempt a new assignment using an older ready snapshot. The target rejects it after local gate closure. Work committed before closure remains subject to the host drain. Deliver the update and verify remote withdrawal of eligibility.

Race readiness with shutdown and repeat shutdown triggers. Once the gate closes, it stays closed and a queued readiness write cannot overwrite applied drain metadata. Exercise failed publication and verify closed admission and bounded shutdown.

Crash a ready node without a final publication. Under the simulator's advancing clock, observe suspicion and loss of eligibility. Restart with a higher generation and verify that replayed or still-live older observations cannot become eligible while higher-generation history is retained. Present an assignment bound to the old generation to the restarted target and verify rejection even once the target is ready.

Partition an observer during a lifecycle change. After healing and allowing gossip and reconciliation to run, verify the observer reflects current eligibility. Pause a subscriber across multiple revisions and confirm that it recovers from the complete latest snapshot, then closes its candidate cache on watch closure.

section.t: For deployment validation, measure time from local readiness or drain transition to observed eligibility change, time from simulated failure to suspicion, and false suspicions of healthy nodes under representative loss and churn. Record node count, network assumptions, and failures to converge within the measurement window with each run. These measurements inform deployment-specific objectives and failure-detector tuning.

section.name: Security Considerations
section.t: Deploy gossip only on a trusted, access-restricted network. Operators MUST restrict gossip UDP access to trusted peers. The cluster ID selects a protocol domain. Chitchat gossip in this implementation has neither peer authentication nor encryption. A sender with network access can forge identity, generation, address, or metadata evidence, suppress usable candidates, or exhaust resources. Application metadata MUST NOT contain secrets. Metadata limits bound individual records. They do not bound all traffic or the number of claimed identities.

Membership, including lifecycle and incarnation information, conveys no request authorization or exclusive ownership. The destination's request authentication and authorization and any ownership fencing belong to their respective contracts. Local incarnation and gate checks address stale selection under the trusted-network assumptions.
